newsitem.title: USA: Dole hits Clinton on ethics, president.
newsitem.headline: Dole hits Clinton on ethics, president.

text.p: With just two days left until Election Day, Republican Bob Dole was predicting victory and continuing to hammer away at President Clinton's ethics as Clinton lamented the use of political insults to win votes.
Dole, still energised despite his lack of sleep, headed for South Dakota and Las Vegas on his second night of round-the-clock campaigning before arriving in California before dawn.

"There is something happening across America ... I think we're going to win this race," Dole told a crowd in Omaha, Nebraska, as he continue to fire away at alleged campaign-finance improprieties and ethical lapses of Clinton's administration.
Dole was in the second day of a non-stop campaign marathon that began on Friday and was to continue until he casts his vote in his hometown of Russell, Kansas, on Tuesday.

The 35-year veteran of Congress is lagging Clinton in the polls -- although several polls show the margin narrowing -- and hopes his marathon tactics will inject enthusiasm into his campaign and swing voters to his side.
Clinton, due to arrive in Tampa, Florida, in the wee hours of Sunday, after a nostalgic visit to his old hometown of Little Rock, Arkansas, where he criticised Dole's attack strategy.

"I really don't like a lot of what's happened in politics in the last several years. I don't like the fact that especially when it gets down toward the end and people get desperate, they think the only thing to do is try to convince you their opponent is no good," he said.

Clinton did not mention Dole by name, but his comments -- in a tone more of sorrow than anger -- clearly referred to his challenger's relentless attacks on his ethics and character in the closing days of the presidential race.
Clinton cancelled an election-eve visit to California, where the election could be decided, in a sign of his confidence that he will prevail on Tuesday.
Instead, the president will focus on last-minute campaigning in Ohio, Kentucky, Iowa and South Dakota.

Clinton's visit to Arkansas -- designed to boost the chances of some Democratic congressional candidates -- also signalled his confidence that he will win re-election on Tuesday even though some polls indicate the race is tightening as the contestants near the finish line.

In the Reuters/Zogby daily tracking poll released on Saturday, Dole had closed the gap between him and Clinton to 3.8 percentage points -- 42.4 percent to 38.6 percent, with Reform Party candidate Ross Perot at 8.4 percent. Other polls, however, show Clinton with a much larger margin.

White House political director Doug Sosnik said the narrowing was to be expected, and did not suggest Dole might pull off an upset. "We tracked last night and we haven't seen any change in the race at all," he said.
Dole, saying he felt confident that an upset was within reach, continued to hit the ethics issue in a last-ditch bid to sway undecided voters.

"We've had literally a scandal a week in this administration the past several weeks," Dole said in Indianapolis. "I think the American people are starting to say 'What's going on there. What's going on in this White House?'"
"If (Clinton's) re-elected he's going to spend half of his time next year with investigations ... who knows what will happen in the next 24 months, 36 months," Dole said.
